topics.title: Energy

subtopics.title: Energy changes in a system, and the ways energy is stored before and after such changes

spec.t: A system is an object or group of objects.
notes: The link between work done (energy transfer) and current flow in a circuit is covered in Energy transfers (page 29).

spec.t: There are changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes.

Students should be able to describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example: • an object projected upwards • a moving object hitting an obstacle • an object accelerated by a constant force • a vehicle slowing down • bringing water to a boil in an electric kettle.
Throughout this section on Energy students should be able to calculate the changes in energy involved when a system is changed by: • heating • work done by forces • work done when a current flows
• use calculations to show on a common scale how the overall energy in a system is redistributed when the system is changed.

los.t: Define a system
k: A system is an object or group of objects.
The link between work done (energy transfer) and current flow in a circuit is covered in Energy transfers (page 29).

los.t: State that the way energy is stored changes when a system changes
k: There are changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes.

Energy stores (names used in AQA questions): kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal (internal), chemical, nuclear, magnetic, electrostatic. Energy is transferred between stores mechanically (by forces), electrically, by heating, and by radiation (waves such as light and sound).
The specification does not list the names of the energy stores or transfer pathways in this section; they are given as explanatory vocabulary used in AQA questions.

los.t: Describe the energy changes when an object is projected upwards
k: Describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example: an object projected upwards.

Kinetic energy store decreases while the gravitational potential energy store increases as the object rises (some energy is dissipated to thermal energy of the surroundings by air resistance). At the top most energy is gravitational potential.

los.t: Describe the energy changes when a moving object hits an obstacle
k: Describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example: a moving object hitting an obstacle.
Kinetic energy store decreases; energy is transferred to thermal energy stores (object, obstacle, surroundings) and sound (waves), and possibly elastic/deformation energy.

los.t: Describe the energy changes when an object is accelerated by a constant force
k: Describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example: an object accelerated by a constant force.
Work done by the force transfers energy to the kinetic energy store of the object (minus some dissipated as thermal energy by friction).

los.t: Describe the energy changes when a vehicle slows down
k: Describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example: a vehicle slowing down.
Kinetic energy store decreases; brakes do work against the wheels, so the thermal energy store of the brakes (and surroundings) increases.

los.t: Describe the energy changes when water is brought to a boil in an electric kettle
k: Describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example: bringing water to a boil in an electric kettle.
Electrical work done by the current → thermal energy store of the heating element → thermal energy store of the water (temperature rises); some is dissipated to the kettle and surroundings.

los.t: Calculate changes in energy caused by heating, work done by forces and work done by a current
k: Throughout this section on Energy students should be able to calculate the changes in energy involved when a system is changed by: heating; work done by forces; work done when a current flows.
Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ (4.1.1.3). Work done by a force: W = Fs (4.5.2). Work done by a current: E = Pt = VIt (4.2.4).

los.t: Use calculations to show on a common scale how overall energy is redistributed
k: Use calculations to show on a common scale how the overall energy in a system is redistributed when the system is changed.
Convert every store to joules and show that energy transferred in = energy stored out + energy dissipated.

spec.t: Students should be able to calculate the amount of energy associated with a moving object, a stretched spring and an object raised above ground level.
The kinetic energy of a moving object can be calculated using the equation: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × speed²
notes: Students should be able to recall and apply this equation.

spec.t: Ek = ½ m v²; kinetic energy, Ek, in joules, J; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; speed, v, in metres per second, m/s
The amount of elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring can be calculated using the equation: elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × extension²
notes: Students should be able to apply this equation which is given on the Physics equation sheet.

spec.t: Ee = ½ k e²
(assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded) elastic potential energy, Ee, in joules, J; spring constant, k, in newtons per metre, N/m; extension, e, in metres, m
The amount of gravitational potential energy gained by an object raised above ground level can be calculated using the equation: g.p.e. = mass × gravitational field strength × height

Ep = m g h; gravitational potential energy, Ep, in joules, J; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg (In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given).
notes: Students should be able to recall and apply this equation.
AT 1 Investigate the transfer of energy from a gravitational potential energy store to a kinetic energy store.

spec.t: height, h, in metres, m

los.t: Calculate the energy of a moving object, a stretched spring and an object raised above ground level
k: Calculate the amount of energy associated with a moving object, a stretched spring and an object raised above ground level.

los.t: Recall and apply the kinetic energy equation
k: The kinetic energy of a moving object can be calculated using the equation: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × speed².
Ek = ½ m v²; kinetic energy, Ek, in joules, J; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; speed, v, in metres per second, m/s.
Students should be able to recall and apply this equation (MS 3b, 3c).
Car of mass 1000 kg at 20 m/s: Ek = 0.5 × 1000 × 20² = 200 000 J. Rearranged: v = √(2Ek ÷ m).
The speed is squared: doubling speed quadruples the kinetic energy.

los.t: Apply the elastic potential energy equation
k: The amount of elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring can be calculated using the equation: elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × extension².
Ee = ½ k e²; elastic potential energy, Ee, in joules, J; spring constant, k, in newtons per metre, N/m; extension, e, in metres, m.
Students should be able to apply this equation, which is given on the Physics equation sheet (MS 3b, 3c).
k = 40 N/m, e = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m: Ee = 0.5 × 40 × 0.050² = 0.050 J. Convert cm → m before substituting.

los.t: State the condition for the elastic potential energy equation
k: (assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded).
Beyond the limit of proportionality force is no longer proportional to extension, so ½ke² no longer gives the stored energy (see 4.5.3).

los.t: Recall and apply the gravitational potential energy equation
k: The amount of gravitational potential energy gained by an object raised above ground level can be calculated using the equation: g.p.e. = mass × gravitational field strength × height.
Ep = m g h; gravitational potential energy, Ep, in joules, J; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg; height, h, in metres, m.
In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.
Students should be able to recall and apply this equation. AT 1 – investigate the transfer of energy from a gravitational potential energy store to a kinetic energy store.
m = 2.0 kg, g = 10 N/kg, h = 3.0 m: Ep = 2.0 × 10 × 3.0 = 60 J. If it falls, ignoring air resistance, Ep → Ek: ½mv² = mgh ⇒ v = √(2gh).
Gravitational field strength on Earth is about 9.8 N/kg (often given as 10 N/kg).

spec.t: The amount of energy stored in or released from a system as its temperature changes can be calculated using the equation: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
notes: Students should be able to apply this equation which is given on the Physics equation sheet.

spec.t: ΔE = m c Δθ; change in thermal energy, ΔE, in joules, J; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; specific heat capacity, c, in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C; temperature change, Δθ, in degrees Celsius, °C
notes: This equation and specific heat capacity are also included in Temperature changes in a system and specific heat capacity (page 34).

spec.t: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.

Required practical activity 1: investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials. The investigation will involve linking the decrease of one energy store (or work done) to the increase in temperature and subsequent increase in thermal energy stored.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 5.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development (page 89).

los.t: Apply the equation for change in thermal energy
k: The amount of energy stored in or released from a system as its temperature changes can be calculated using the equation: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change.

ΔE = m c Δθ; change in thermal energy, ΔE, in joules, J; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; specific heat capacity, c, in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C; temperature change, Δθ, in degrees Celsius, °C.
Students should be able to apply this equation, which is given on the Physics equation sheet (MS 3b, 3c).
This equation and specific heat capacity are also included in Temperature changes in a system and specific heat capacity (page 34).
Heating 2.0 kg of water by 10 °C (c = 4200 J/kg °C): ΔE = 2.0 × 4200 × 10 = 84 000 J. Convert g → kg first.

los.t: Define specific heat capacity
k: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.
A high specific heat capacity means a lot of energy is needed per kg per °C (e.g. water 4200 J/kg °C).

los.t: Required practical 1 – specific heat capacity
k: Required practical activity 1: investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials. The investigation will involve linking the decrease of one energy store (or work done) to the increase in temperature and subsequent increase in thermal energy stored.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 5.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development (page 89).
Full detail in Part C – Required Practical 1.

spec.t: Power is defined as the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done.
notes: Students should be able to recall and apply both equations.

spec.t: power = energy transferred ÷ time, P = E / t; power = work done ÷ time, P = W / t; power, P, in watts, W; energy transferred, E, in joules, J; time, t, in seconds, s; work done, W, in joules, J
An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt.

Students should be able to give examples that illustrate the definition of power eg comparing two electric motors that both lift the same weight through the same height but one does it faster than the other.

los.t: Define power and recall both power equations
k: Power is defined as the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done.
Students should be able to recall and apply both equations (MS 3b, 3c).

los.t: Apply the power equations
k: power = energy transferred ÷ time (P = E / t); power = work done ÷ time (P = W / t).
power, P, in watts, W; energy transferred, E, in joules, J; time, t, in seconds, s; work done, W, in joules, J.
A motor transfers 600 J in 20 s: P = 600 ÷ 20 = 30 W. Rearranged: E = Pt; t = E ÷ P.

los.t: State the unit definition of the watt
k: An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt.

los.t: Give examples that illustrate the definition of power
k: Give examples that illustrate the definition of power eg comparing two electric motors that both lift the same weight through the same height but one does it faster than the other.
Same work done (same weight × same height) but the faster motor does it in less time, so it has the greater power.

spec.t: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.
Students should be able to describe with examples where there are energy transfers in a closed system, that there is no net change to the total energy.
Students should be able to describe, with examples, how in all system changes energy is dissipated, so that it is stored in less useful ways. This energy is often described as being ‘wasted’.
Students should be able to explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfers, for example through lubrication and the use of thermal insulation.
notes: Investigate thermal conductivity using rods of different materials.

spec.t: The higher the thermal conductivity of a material the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material.
Students should be able to describe how the rate of cooling of a building is affected by the thickness and thermal conductivity of its walls.
Students do not need to know the definition of thermal conductivity.

Required practical activity 2 (physics only): investigate the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators and the factors that may affect the thermal insulation properties of a material.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 5.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development (page 90).

los.t: State that energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated but not created or destroyed
k: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.
Conservation of energy: the total energy of a closed system is constant.

los.t: Describe with examples that a closed system has no net change in total energy
k: Describe with examples where there are energy transfers in a closed system, that there is no net change to the total energy.

los.t: Describe with examples how energy is dissipated
k: Describe, with examples, how in all system changes energy is dissipated, so that it is stored in less useful ways.
This energy is often described as being ‘wasted’.
Bulb: electrical energy → light (useful) + thermal energy of surroundings (wasted). Dissipated energy spreads out in thermal energy stores of the surroundings.

los.t: Explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfers
k: Explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfers, for example through lubrication and the use of thermal insulation.
WS 1.4; AT 1, 5 – investigate thermal conductivity using rods of different materials.

Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts, so less energy is dissipated as heat. Thermal insulation (e.g. cavity wall insulation, loft insulation) reduces the rate of energy transfer by conduction (and convection/radiation).

los.t: State the relationship between thermal conductivity and rate of energy transfer by conduction
k: The higher the thermal conductivity of a material the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material.

los.t: Describe how the rate of cooling of a building depends on wall thickness and thermal conductivity
k: Describe how the rate of cooling of a building is affected by the thickness and thermal conductivity of its walls.
Thicker walls and lower thermal conductivity → slower rate of cooling; thin walls of high conductivity → faster cooling.

los.t: Know that the definition of thermal conductivity is not required
k: Students do not need to know the definition of thermal conductivity.

los.t: Required practical 2 – thermal insulators
k: Required practical activity 2 (physics only): investigate the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators and the factors that may affect the thermal insulation properties of a material.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 5.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development (page 90).
Full detail in Part C – Required Practical 2.

spec.t: The energy efficiency for any energy transfer can be calculated using the equation: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer. Efficiency may also be calculated using the equation: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input
notes: Students should be able to recall and apply both equations.
Students may be required to calculate or use efficiency values as a decimal or as a percentage.

spec.t: (HT only) Students should be able to describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer.

los.t: Calculate efficiency from energy transfers
k: The energy efficiency for any energy transfer can be calculated using the equation: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer.
Students should be able to recall and apply both equations (MS 3b, 3c).
A motor takes in 200 J and transfers 80 J usefully: efficiency = 80 ÷ 200 = 0.40 = 40%.

los.t: Calculate efficiency from power
k: Efficiency may also be calculated using the equation: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input.
Input 50 W, useful output 35 W: efficiency = 0.70 (70%).

los.t: Use efficiency values as a decimal or a percentage
k: Students may be required to calculate or use efficiency values as a decimal or as a percentage (MS 1a, 1c, 3b, 3c).
Efficiency is never greater than 1 (100%) – energy cannot be created. Percentage = decimal × 100.

los.t: Describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer
k: (HT only) Students should be able to describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer.
Lubricate moving parts, insulate to reduce heat loss, use materials of low resistance/ better design to reduce friction, air resistance and heating effect of currents.

spec.t: The main energy resources available for use on Earth include: fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves.
A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
The uses of energy resources include: transport, electricity generation and heating.

Students should be able to: • describe the main energy sources available • distinguish between energy resources that are renewable and energy resources that are non-renewable • compare ways that different energy resources are used, the uses to include transport, electricity generation and heating • understand why some energy resources are more reliable than others
• describe the environmental impact arising from the use of different energy resources
• explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources.
Descriptions of how energy resources are used to generate electricity are not required.

Students should be able to: • consider the environmental issues that may arise from the use of different energy resources • show that science has the ability to identify environmental issues arising from the use of energy resources but not always the power to deal with the issues because of political, social, ethical or economic considerations.

los.t: List the main energy resources available on Earth
k: The main energy resources available for use on Earth include: fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves.

los.t: Define a renewable energy resource
k: A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.

los.t: State the uses of energy resources
k: The uses of energy resources include: transport, electricity generation and heating.

los.t: Describe the main energy sources available
k: Describe the main energy sources available.

Fossil fuels – burn to release thermal energy. Nuclear fuel – fission. Bio-fuel – burn plant/animal material. Wind – turbines. Hydroelectricity – falling water. Geothermal – hot rocks. Tides – rising/falling sea. Sun – solar cells/panels. Water waves – movement of waves.

los.t: Distinguish renewable from non-renewable resources
k: Distinguish between energy resources that are renewable and energy resources that are non-renewable.
Non-renewable: coal, oil, gas, nuclear fuel (finite). Renewable: bio-fuel, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, tides, Sun, waves.

los.t: Compare ways that different energy resources are used (transport, electricity, heating)
k: Compare ways that different energy resources are used, the uses to include transport, electricity generation and heating.

los.t: Explain why some energy resources are more reliable than others
k: Understand why some energy resources are more reliable than others.

Reliable = available whenever needed: fossil fuels, nuclear, biofuel, geothermal, hydro (with storage). Less reliable: wind (wind speed), solar (daylight/cloud), waves, tides (predictable but varying).

los.t: Describe the environmental impact of different energy resources
k: Describe the environmental impact arising from the use of different energy resources.

Fossil fuels – CO2 (global warming), SO2 (acid rain); nuclear – radioactive waste; wind – visual/noise/habitat; hydro – flooding habitats; tidal – estuary ecosystems; solar – land use and manufacture; bio-fuel – land use/ habitats.

los.t: Explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources
k: Explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources.
Use data given: reasons include cost, availability, reliability, political decisions, climate concerns and technology developments.

los.t: Know that descriptions of electricity generation are not required
k: Descriptions of how energy resources are used to generate electricity are not required.

los.t: Consider environmental issues from the use of different energy resources
k: Consider the environmental issues that may arise from the use of different energy resources.

los.t: Show that science can identify environmental issues but not always solve them due to political, social, ethical or economic considerations
k: Show that science has the ability to identify environmental issues arising from the use of energy resources but not always the power to deal with the issues because of political, social, ethical or economic considerations.

overview: The concept of energy emerged in the 19th century. The idea was used to explain the work output of steam engines and then generalised to understand other heat engines. It also became a key tool for understanding chemical reactions and biological systems.
Limits to the use of fossil fuels and global warming are critical problems for this century. Physicists and engineers are working hard to identify ways to reduce our energy usage.

topics.title: Electricity

spec.t: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols. [Figure in specification — standard circuit symbols: switch (open), switch (closed), cell, battery, diode, resistor, variable resistor, LED, lamp, fuse, voltmeter, ammeter, thermistor, LDR]
Students should be able to draw and interpret circuit diagrams.

los.t: Recall the standard circuit symbols
k: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols (figure in specification): switch (open), switch (closed), cell, battery, diode, resistor, variable resistor, LED, lamp, fuse, voltmeter, ammeter, thermistor, LDR.
Cell = one pair of lines (long line positive); battery = two or more cells in series. A voltmeter connects in parallel across a component; an ammeter in series.

los.t: Draw circuit diagrams
k: Students should be able to draw circuit diagrams.
Use a ruler, complete closed loops, correct symbols, no gaps or symbols drawn on corners.

los.t: Interpret circuit diagrams
k: Students should be able to interpret circuit diagrams.

spec.t: For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference.

Electric current is a flow of electrical charge. The size of the electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge. Charge flow, current and time are linked by the equation: charge flow = current × time
notes: Students should be able to recall and apply this equation.

spec.t: Q = I t; charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C; current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere); time, t, in seconds, s
A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop.

los.t: State that a source of potential difference is needed for charge to flow in a closed circuit
k: For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference.

los.t: Define electric current
k: Electric current is a flow of electrical charge.
The size of the electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge.
In metals the charge carriers are electrons (negatively charged); conventional current is drawn from + to –.

los.t: Recall and apply the charge flow equation
k: Charge flow, current and time are linked by the equation: charge flow = current × time.
Q = I t; charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C; current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere); time, t, in seconds, s.
Students should be able to recall and apply this equation (MS 3b, 3c).
2.0 A for 30 s: Q = 2.0 × 30 = 60 C. Rearranged: I = Q ÷ t; t = Q ÷ I. Convert minutes to seconds first.

los.t: State that current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop
k: A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop.

spec.t: The current (I) through a component depends on both the resistance (R) of the component and the potential difference (V) across the component. The greater the resistance of the component the smaller the current for a given potential difference (pd) across the component.
Questions will be set using the term potential difference. Students will gain credit for the correct use of either potential difference or voltage.
Current, potential difference or resistance can be calculated using the equation: potential difference = current × resistance
notes: Students should be able to recall and apply this equation.

spec.t: V = I R; potential difference, V, in volts, V; current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere); resistance, R, in ohms, Ω

Required practical activity 3: Use circuit diagrams to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits. This should include: • the length of a wire at constant temperature • combinations of resistors in series and parallel.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 6 and 7.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development (page 91).

los.t: Relate current to resistance and potential difference
k: The current (I) through a component depends on both the resistance (R) of the component and the potential difference (V) across the component.
The greater the resistance of the component the smaller the current for a given potential difference (pd) across the component.

los.t: Use the terms potential difference and voltage
k: Questions will be set using the term potential difference.
Students will gain credit for the correct use of either potential difference or voltage.

los.t: Recall and apply the V = IR equation
k: Current, potential difference or resistance can be calculated using the equation: potential difference = current × resistance.
V = I R; potential difference, V, in volts, V; current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere); resistance, R, in ohms, Ω.
Students should be able to recall and apply this equation (MS 3b, 3c).
12 V across 4.0 Ω: I = V ÷ R = 3.0 A. Rearranged: R = V ÷ I; V = IR. Convert mA → A, kΩ → Ω.

los.t: Required practical 3 – factors affecting resistance
k: Required practical activity 3: Use circuit diagrams to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits. This should include: the length of a wire at constant temperature; combinations of resistors in series and parallel.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 6 and 7.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development (page 91).
Full detail in Part C – Required Practical 3.

spec.t: Students should be able to explain that, for some resistors, the value of R remains constant but that in others it can change as the current changes.

The current through an ohmic conductor (at a constant temperature) is directly proportional to the potential difference across the resistor. This means that the resistance remains constant as the current changes. [Figure in specification — I–V graph (current on the vertical axis, potential difference on the horizontal axis): a straight line through the origin, extending into both positive and negative values]
The resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant; it changes with the current through the component.

The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases. [Figure in specification — I–V graph for a filament lamp: an S-shaped curve through the origin; the gradient decreases (the curve flattens) as potential difference increases in either direction]

The current through a diode flows in one direction only. The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction. [Figure in specification — I–V graph for a diode: current is zero for negative potential difference and (almost) zero for small positive potential difference, then rises steeply]
The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases.
The applications of thermistors in circuits eg a thermostat is required.
The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.
The application of LDRs in circuits eg switching lights on when it gets dark is required.

Students should be able to: • explain the design and use of a circuit to measure the resistance of a component by measuring the current through, and potential difference across, the component • draw an appropriate circuit diagram using correct circuit symbols.
notes: Investigate the relationship between the resistance of a thermistor and temperature.
Investigate the relationship between the resistance of an LDR and light intensity.

spec.t: Students should be able to use graphs to explore whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear and relate the curves produced to their function and properties.

Required practical activity 4: use circuit diagrams to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I–V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 6 and 7.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development (page 93).

los.t: Explain that for some resistors R is constant and for others it changes with current
k: Explain that, for some resistors, the value of R remains constant but that in others it can change as the current changes.

los.t: Describe ohmic conductors
k: The current through an ohmic conductor (at a constant temperature) is directly proportional to the potential difference across the resistor.
This means that the resistance remains constant as the current changes. I–V graph: straight line through the origin (figure in specification).

los.t: State that resistance of lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant
k: The resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant; it changes with the current through the component.

los.t: Describe the filament lamp
k: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases.
I–V graph: an S-shaped curve (figure in specification).
More current → hotter filament → metal ions vibrate more → more collisions with electrons → higher resistance → graph curves (non-linear).

los.t: Describe the diode
k: The current through a diode flows in one direction only.
The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.
I–V graph: zero current in the reverse direction, rising steeply in the forward direction (figure in specification).

los.t: Describe the thermistor
k: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases.

los.t: State applications of thermistors in circuits
k: The applications of thermistors in circuits eg a thermostat is required.
Thermostats, fire alarms, car engine temperature sensors.

los.t: Describe the LDR
k: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.

los.t: State applications of LDRs in circuits
k: The application of LDRs in circuits eg switching lights on when it gets dark is required.

los.t: Explain the design and use of a circuit to measure resistance
k: Explain the design and use of a circuit to measure the resistance of a component by measuring the current through, and potential difference across, the component.
AT 6 – investigate the relationship between the resistance of a thermistor and temperature; and between the resistance of an LDR and light intensity.
Component in series with an ammeter and variable resistor (to vary current), power supply and switch; voltmeter in parallel across the component. R = V ÷ I.

spec.t: There are two ways of joining electrical components, in series and in parallel. Some circuits include both series and parallel parts.

For components connected in series: • there is the same current through each component • the total potential difference of the power supply is shared between the components • the total resistance of two components is the sum of the resistance of each component.
R_total = R₁ + R₂; resistance, R, in ohms, Ω

For components connected in parallel: • the potential difference across each component is the same • the total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components • the total resistance of two resistors is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.

overview: Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter everywhere. Understanding the difference in the microstructure of conductors, semiconductors and insulators makes it possible to design components and build electric circuits. Many circuits are powered with mains electricity, but portable electrical devices must use batteries of some kind.

Electrical power fills the modern world with artificial light and sound, information and entertainment, remote sensing and control. The fundamentals of electromagnetism were worked out by scientists of the 19th century. However, power stations, like all machines, have a limited lifetime. If we all continue to demand more electricity this means building new power stations in every generation – but what mix of power stations can promise a sustainable future?

groups.title: The development of the model of the atom (common content with chemistry)

spec.t: New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
notes: This historical context provides an opportunity for students to show an understanding of why and describe how scientific methods and theories develop over time.

spec.t: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model of the atom. The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

The results from the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged. This nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge. The name proton was given to these particles.
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
Students should be able to describe: • why the new evidence from the scattering experiment led to a change in the atomic model
• the difference between the plum pudding model of the atom and the nuclear model of the atom.
Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
Details of Chadwick’s experimental work are not required.

spec.t: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. The nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. This is a random process called radioactive decay.
Activity is the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays.
Activity is measured in becquerel (Bq)
Count-rate is the number of decays recorded each second by a detector (eg Geiger-Muller tube).

The nuclear radiation emitted may be: • an alpha particle (α) – this consists of two neutrons and two protons, it is the same as a helium nucleus • a beta particle (β) – a high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton • a gamma ray (γ) – electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus • a neutron (n).
Required knowledge of the properties of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays is limited to their penetration through materials, their range in air and ionising power.
Students should be able to apply their knowledge to the uses of radiation and evaluate the best sources of radiation to use in a given situation.

spec.t: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus (eg uranium or plutonium).
Spontaneous fission is rare. Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, and emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays. Energy is released by the fission reaction.
All of the fission products have kinetic energy.
The neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction.
The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released. The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.

overview: Ionising radiation is hazardous but can be very useful. Although radioactivity was discovered over a century ago, it took many nuclear physicists several decades to understand the structure of atoms, nuclear forces and stability. Today radioactive materials are widely used in medicine, industry, agriculture and electrical power generation.

spec.t: Students should be able to explain in qualitative terms, how the differences in velocity, absorption and reflection between different types of wave in solids and liquids can be used both for detection and exploration of structures which are hidden from direct observation.

Ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Ultrasound waves are partially reflected when they meet a boundary between two different media. The time taken for the reflections to reach a detector can be used to determine how far away such a boundary is. This allows ultrasound waves to be used for both medical and industrial imaging.

Echo sounding, using high frequency sound waves is used to detect objects in deep water and measure water depth.
Students should be aware that the study of seismic waves provided new evidence that led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.

spec.t: The poles of a magnet are the places where the magnetic forces are strongest. When two magnets are brought close together they exert a force on each other. Two like poles repel each other. Two unlike poles attract each other. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force.

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field. An induced magnet is a material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction. When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most/all of its magnetism quickly.

spec.t: The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt and nickel) is called the magnetic field.
The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.
The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet. The field is strongest at the poles of the magnet.

The direction of the magnetic field at any point is given by the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point. The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole of the magnet.
A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet. The Earth has a magnetic field. The compass needle points in the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field.

spec.t: There is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies. The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. This effect is called red-shift.

overview: Questions about where we are, and where we came from, have been asked for thousands of years. In the past century, astronomers and astrophysicists have made remarkable progress in understanding the scale and structure of the universe, its evolution and ours. New questions have emerged recently. ‘Dark matter’, which bends light and holds galaxies together but does not emit electromagnetic radiation, is everywhere – what is it? And what is causing the universe to expand ever faster?

spec.t: The complex and diverse phenomena of the natural and man-made world can be described in terms of a small number of key ideas in physics.

These key ideas are of universal application, and we have embedded them throughout the subject content. They underpin many aspects of the science assessment and will therefore be assessed across all papers.

Key ideas in physics include: • the use of models, as in the particle model of matter or the wave models of light and of sound • the concept of cause and effect in explaining such links as those between force and acceleration, or between changes in atomic nuclei and radioactive emissions • the phenomena of ‘action at a distance’ and the related concept of the field as the key to analysing electrical, magnetic and gravitational effects • that differences, for example between pressures or temperatures or electrical potentials, are the drivers of change • that proportionality, for example between weight and mass of an object or between force and extension in a spring, is an important aspect of many models in science • that physical laws and models are expressed in mathematical form.

PURPOSE: To determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials by linking the energy transferred by an electrical heater (the decrease of one energy store, or work done) to the increase in temperature of the material and the increase in thermal energy stored in it (4.1.1.3).
APPARATUS: 1 kg (or 500 g) block of metal (e.g. aluminium) with one hole for a heater and one for a thermometer; or a polystyrene cup of water for a liquid
Electric immersion heater (e.g. 50 W, 12 V) and low-voltage power supply (or a joulemeter)
Ammeter and voltmeter (if no joulemeter), leads, switch
Thermometer (or temperature probe and data logger), a little oil/water for thermal contact in the thermometer hole
Balance (to measure the mass), stopwatch
Insulation (e.g. cotton wool, bubble wrap or a lagging jacket) around the block, lid for the cup
Eye protection
METHOD: Measure the mass of the block (or of the water) with a balance and record it in kg.
Place the heater in the larger hole and the thermometer in the other hole; add a drop of oil so there is good thermal contact. Wrap the block in insulation.
Record the starting temperature.
Connect the heater to the power supply with the ammeter in series and the voltmeter across the heater (or use a joulemeter). Switch on and start the stopwatch at the same moment.
Record the temperature every 60 s for about 10 minutes (or until it has risen by about 15–25 °C). Keep the current and potential difference constant; record them.
Switch off the heater but keep watching the thermometer; the temperature continues to rise for a short time because the heater is still hot. Record the highest temperature reached.
Calculate the energy supplied: E = P t = V I t (or read the joulemeter) at each time. Plot energy transferred (y-axis) against temperature rise (x-axis).
The gradient = m c, so c = gradient ÷ m. Alternatively, calculate c = ΔE ÷ (m Δθ) using the final values.
Repeat with a different material (or a different mass) to compare.
IV: The material (or the energy supplied to it).
DV: The temperature rise of the material.
CV: Mass of the material
Power of the heater (current and pd)
Starting temperature
Insulation and position of the thermometer
SAFETY: Heater, block and water become hot enough to burn – do not touch; allow to cool before handling.
Keep electrical leads and connections away from water; do not run the immersion heater in air or out of the hole in the block.
Do not exceed the heater's rated pd; switch off if anything smells hot.
Wear eye protection; use a low-voltage supply.
RESULTS: Temperature rises steadily with time (energy supplied), giving an approximately straight energy–temperature graph.

Typical values: aluminium about 900 J/kg °C; water about 4200 J/kg °C. Measured values usually come out too high because some energy is lost to the surroundings (so more energy is needed than is stored in the block).
ANALYSIS: Energy supplied E = P t = V I t (units: J, W, s, V, A).
Specific heat capacity c = ΔE ÷ (m Δθ), from ΔE = m c Δθ (J/kg °C).
Example: 50 W for 600 s gives 30 000 J; a 1.0 kg block rising by 33 °C gives c = 30 000 ÷ (1.0 × 33) ≈ 910 J/kg °C.
Using the gradient of an energy–temperature graph is better than a single calculation because it averages repeat readings and shows anomalies.
ERRORS: Energy is lost to the surroundings, so the temperature rise is smaller than it should be and c is overestimated. Improve by insulating the block well, using a lid, and keeping the heating time short.
Poor thermal contact between the thermometer and the block – use oil/water in the thermometer hole and wait for the temperature to settle.
The temperature continues to rise after the heater is switched off – record the maximum temperature.
The resolution of the thermometer (±0.5 °C) and the reaction time of the stopwatch – use a larger temperature rise, a data logger or temperature probe.
EXAM: Which energy store decreases and which increases? (Energy supplied electrically from the supply/work done by the supply; thermal energy store of the block increases.)
Why insulate the block? Why use oil? Why record the highest temperature after switching off?
Calculate c from data; rearrange ΔE = m c Δθ; convert minutes to seconds and g to kg.
Define specific heat capacity (4.1.1.3 / 4.3.2.2). Link: AT 1, AT 5; equation given on the sheet.
State why the experiment gives a value of c that is higher than the accepted value.

PURPOSE: (Physics only) To investigate the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators and the factors that may affect the thermal insulation properties of a material, such as thickness (4.1.2.1).
APPARATUS: Beaker or insulated container (same size for each material) with a lid
Different insulating materials (e.g. newspaper, bubble wrap, cotton wool, foam, felt, fabric)
Hot water (e.g. about 80 °C from a kettle), measuring cylinder
Thermometer (or temperature probe and data logger), stopwatch, elastic bands/tape
Ruler or micrometer for thickness
Eye protection
METHOD: Wrap the first material around the beaker (same number of layers/thickness each time) and secure it with tape.
Measure the same volume of hot water (e.g. 100 cm³) and pour it into the beaker; record the starting temperature (the same each time, e.g. 80 °C). Fit the lid and put the thermometer through the lid.
Start the stopwatch and record the temperature every minute for about 10–15 minutes.
Repeat with each material; also repeat with an unwrapped beaker as a control.
To investigate a second factor, repeat with one material using different thicknesses (e.g. 1, 2, 3 layers) or a different surface area.
Plot temperature (y) against time (x) for each material (cooling curves) or calculate the temperature drop in a fixed time.
IV: The type of insulating material (then, separately, its thickness or number of layers).
DV: The fall in temperature of the water (°C) in a fixed time, or the time taken to cool by a fixed amount.
CV: Volume and starting temperature of the water
Size and material of the container; lid used or not
Thickness of the insulating layer (when comparing materials)
Room temperature and time interval
SAFETY: Hot water scalds: carry it carefully, keep containers stable on the bench and do not overfill; clear up spills immediately.
Wear eye protection; do not lean over hot water.
RESULTS: The unwrapped beaker cools fastest. Materials that trap air (e.g. cotton wool, bubble wrap, foam) cool slowest – best insulators; thicker layers reduce the rate of cooling further.
Cooling curves are steepest at the start, when the temperature difference from the surroundings is greatest.
ANALYSIS: Temperature drop = start − end temperature; compare drops in the same time, or compare the time taken to fall by the same amount.
Rate of cooling = temperature change ÷ time (gradient of the curve); use tangents on curves (MS 4e).
Best insulator = smallest temperature drop / lowest rate of energy transfer (4.1.2.1).
ERRORS: Starting temperatures not identical – measure each starting temperature and compare temperature drops, or start each run from the same temperature.
Draughts, room temperature changes, and uneven wrapping – use lids and the same arrangement each time.
Thermometer resolution – use a temperature probe and data logger.
Only one repeat – repeat three times and calculate a mean.
EXAM: Why is it a fair test to use the same volume and starting temperature of water? Why use a lid?
Draw/interpret cooling curves; state which material is best; give a conclusion linked to the data.

Link to 4.1.2.1 (reducing unwanted energy transfers: lubrication, thermal insulation; thermal conductivity; thicker walls, lower thermal conductivity = lower rate of energy transfer by conduction). Link: AT 1, AT 5.

PURPOSE: To use circuit diagrams to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits – the length of a wire at constant temperature, and combinations of resistors in series and parallel (4.2.1.3).
APPARATUS: Resistance wire (e.g. constantan or nichrome, about 1 m) taped to a metre rule; crocodile clips
Low-voltage power supply or cells (e.g. 2–4 V), switch, connecting leads
Ammeter (in series) and voltmeter (in parallel across the wire)
For combinations: several known resistors (e.g. 10 Ω, 20 Ω)
Eye protection
METHOD: Part 1 – length: set up a series circuit (power supply, switch, ammeter, wire) and connect the voltmeter across the length of wire between two crocodile clips.
Set the length to 10 cm; switch on, record the current and pd, then switch off at once (so the wire does not heat up).
Increase the length in 10 cm steps up to 100 cm, recording I and V each time; repeat the readings and take means.
Calculate resistance R = V ÷ I for each length. Plot R (y) against length (x).
Part 2 – combinations: construct a circuit with two resistors in series; measure the current and pd across the pair and calculate the total resistance; compare with R₁ + R₂.
Repeat with the resistors in parallel (and with more resistors) and compare the total resistance with the individual resistances.
IV: Length of wire (part 1); arrangement/number of resistors – series or parallel (part 2).
DV: Resistance of the wire or combination, calculated from V ÷ I.
CV: Temperature of the wire (low current, switch off between readings)
Material and diameter (cross-section) of the wire
Power supply pd
SAFETY: A wire carrying a large current heats up and can burn – use low pd, short readings and switch off between readings.
Do not use mains-powered equipment with wet hands; check leads are not damaged.
Wear eye protection if wires could spring.
RESULTS: Resistance of the wire is directly proportional to its length: a straight line through the origin on a graph of R against length (doubling the length doubles the resistance).
Series: total resistance is the sum of the resistances (greater than either one). Parallel: the total resistance is smaller than the smallest resistor.
ANALYSIS: R = V ÷ I (V = I R rearranged); plot R against length; the gradient = resistance per unit length (Ω per m).
Series check: R_total = R₁ + R₂. Parallel: current splits, the pd across each branch is the same, the total current is the sum of the branch currents (4.2.2).
Example: V = 3.0 V, I = 0.25 A gives R = 12 Ω.
ERRORS: Wire heating changes its resistance (and gives a curved/higher result) – use a small current, switch off between readings.
Contact resistance and poor contact at crocodile clips; zero errors on the meters – check meters read zero, make firm contacts.
Length measurement and parallax – read the rule at eye level; use the same clip positions.
Lead resistance – use a fixed pair of leads, or measure the resistance of the leads.
EXAM: Why switch off between readings? (To keep the wire at constant temperature.)
Where does the voltmeter go? Where does the ammeter go? Draw the circuit diagram with correct symbols.
Calculate resistance from V and I; explain the graph shape; predict the resistance of double the length.
Explain qualitatively why adding resistors in series increases and in parallel decreases the total resistance. Link: AT 1, AT 6, AT 7.

PURPOSE: To use circuit diagrams to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I–V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature (4.2.1.4).
APPARATUS: Variable power supply (or cells with a variable resistor as a potential divider/rheostat), switch
Ammeter (in series with the component) and voltmeter (in parallel across the component)
Components to test: fixed resistor, filament lamp, diode (with a protective resistor in series for the diode)
Connecting leads
METHOD: Draw and build a circuit with the component, ammeter, power supply, switch and variable resistor in series, with the voltmeter in parallel across the component.
Start from 0 V. Increase the pd in steps (e.g. 0.5 V or by adjusting the variable resistor) and record the current and the pd for each step.
Switch off between readings if the component heats up (e.g. the resistor) and let it cool.
Reverse the connections to the component (swap the terminals of the power supply or the component) and repeat to obtain readings for negative pd and current.
Plot I (y-axis) against V (x-axis) for each component and draw a smooth line or curve through the points.
Repeat for each component (resistor, lamp, diode) using the same method.
IV: The potential difference across the component.
CV: The component being tested
Temperature of the resistor (keep current small; switch off between readings)
Same meters and range
SAFETY: Do not exceed the rated pd of the lamp or the maximum forward current of the diode (use the protective resistor).
Lamps become hot; wires may heat up – do not touch.
Keep the maximum pd low and check all connections before switching on.
RESULTS: Fixed resistor (constant temperature): a straight line through the origin (ohmic) – the current is directly proportional to the pd; resistance is constant.
Filament lamp: an S-shaped curve – the gradient decreases as V increases, so resistance increases with temperature.
Diode: negligible current in the reverse direction and for small forward pd; above a threshold forward pd the current rises steeply (very high reverse resistance).
ANALYSIS: R = V ÷ I at any point (not the gradient for non-linear components).
For the resistor, 1 ÷ gradient = resistance.
State whether each element is linear or non-linear and relate the curve to its function (MS 4c, 4d, 4e).
ERRORS: Heating of the resistor/wire alters its resistance – use small currents and switch off between readings.
Meter zero errors and resolution; reading the meters while values fluctuate – wait for a steady reading.
Too few readings near the curve's turning points – take more readings where the graph bends (e.g. near 0.6 V for the diode).
Improvement: use a data logger, repeat and average; use finer pd steps.
EXAM: Draw the circuit diagram for the experiment (voltmeter parallel, ammeter series, variable resistor).
Sketch/interpret the three I–V graphs; explain the shape for the lamp (resistance rises with temperature).
Why must the resistor be kept at constant temperature? Why is a protective resistor used with the diode? Link: AT 6, AT 7.

PURPOSE: To use appropriate apparatus to make and record the measurements needed to determine the densities of regular and irregular solid objects and liquids (4.3.1.1). Volume is found from dimensions for regular objects and by displacement for irregular ones.
APPARATUS: Ruler, micrometer or Vernier callipers (to measure dimensions)
Top-pan balance (mass)
Regularly shaped solids (cuboid, cylinder, sphere) and an irregular solid (e.g. a stone)
Eureka (displacement) can, measuring cylinder, water, string
Liquid (e.g. water, salt solution, oil), beaker or measuring cylinder (25 cm³ or 100 cm³)
METHOD: Regular solid: measure the mass m of the object with the balance. Measure the dimensions several times with the ruler/callipers/micrometer; calculate volume (cuboid V = l × w × h; cylinder V = π r² h). Density ρ = m ÷ V.

Irregular solid: measure its mass. Fill the eureka can with water until it just overflows from the spout; place a measuring cylinder under the spout; lower the object (on a string) gently into the can; the volume of water that collects equals the volume of the object. Read the volume at the meniscus at eye level. Alternative: measure the rise in water level in a measuring cylinder.

Liquid: measure the mass of an empty measuring cylinder (or beaker). Add a measured volume of liquid (e.g. 25 cm³) reading the bottom of the meniscus at eye level; measure the new mass; mass of liquid = difference. Density = mass ÷ volume. Repeat with different volumes and plot mass against volume; the gradient = density.
Repeat measurements and calculate mean densities.
IV: None for a single object (a measurement) – or the volume of liquid if a graph is plotted.
DV: Mass and volume of the object/liquid (so density).
CV: Same balance and measuring equipment; same temperature of the liquid
Zero the balance with any container before each measurement
SAFETY: Lower objects into the displacement can gently to avoid splashing; mop up spills.
Handle heavy objects with care; keep glassware away from the bench edge.
Wash hands if using a salt solution or oil.
RESULTS: Density of the pure material is constant: e.g. water 1.00 g/cm³ (1000 kg/m³); aluminium about 2.7 g/cm³; iron about 7.9 g/cm³ (typical). The mass–volume graph for a liquid is a straight line through the origin.
ANALYSIS: Density ρ = m ÷ V. Check units: g/cm³ × 1000 = kg/m³ (convert cm³ → m³ ÷ 1 000 000 and g → kg ÷ 1000 if required).
Example: 156 g, 20 cm³: ρ = 7.8 g/cm³ = 7800 kg/m³.
ERRORS: Air bubbles trapped on an irregular object or in the liquid – tap it free before reading.
Meniscus read from the wrong angle (parallax) – read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus.
Dimension measurement errors – measure at several places and take a mean; use callipers/micrometer; check for a zero error.
Water left on the object or spilled during displacement – dry the object, use a clean can.
Balance not zeroed – zero before every reading.
EXAM: Describe how to find the density of a regular solid, an irregular solid and a liquid.
Why does the water level rise by the volume of the object? Why read the meniscus at eye level?
Calculate ρ = m ÷ V and convert units. Use the particle model to explain differences in density (4.3.1.1). Link: AT 1.

PURPOSE: To investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring (4.5.3), showing direct proportionality below the limit of proportionality and allowing the spring constant to be found.
APPARATUS: Spring, clamp stand with boss and clamp (base weighted or G-clamped)
Set of identical slotted masses (e.g. 100 g, each giving a weight of about 1 N) and a mass hanger
Metre rule (mm scale) fixed vertically next to the spring, with a pointer or set square
Eye protection
METHOD: Hang the spring from the clamp. Measure its original (unstretched) length l₀ with the ruler at eye level.
Add a 100 g mass (weight about 1.0 N; use g given in the question), wait for the spring to stop moving, and measure the new length.
Repeat, adding one mass at a time up to about 6–8 masses (keep within the elastic region).
Calculate the extension e = l − l₀ for each force (force = weight = m g).
Optionally remove masses one at a time and measure the length again to check that the spring returns to its original length (elastic behaviour).
Plot force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis) and draw a line of best fit through the linear region.
CV: The spring used (same spring each time)
Method of measuring length: same ruler, same starting point
Temperature
SAFETY: Wear eye protection: a stretched spring can snap back and masses can fall.
Keep feet away from beneath the masses; secure the clamp stand firmly.
Do not overload the spring beyond the limit of proportionality.
RESULTS: Extension is directly proportional to force up to the limit of proportionality: a straight line through the origin. Beyond this point, the graph curves (non-linear) and the spring may not return to its original length (inelastic deformation).
ANALYSIS: F = k e. Spring constant k = gradient of the force–extension graph (N/m) in the linear region (convert cm → m).
Work done (elastic potential energy stored) = ½ k e² (4.5.3), or the area under the force–extension graph.
Example: gradient 25 N/m. Extension of 0.040 m stores E = 0.5 × 25 × 0.040² = 0.020 J.
ERRORS: Parallax when reading the ruler – read at eye level, use a pointer/marker at the bottom of the spring.
Ruler not vertical or spring oscillating when read – use a set square, wait for it to settle.
Original length measured inconsistently; mass slightly inaccurate; hanger's mass forgotten – include the hanger in the force.
Spring permanently stretched during the experiment – do not exceed the elastic limit; check the final length.
EXAM: Why use several masses and plot a graph? Why is extension (not length) plotted?
Identify the limit of proportionality; calculate k from the gradient; calculate energy stored (E = ½ k e²).
Distinguish linear from non-linear and elastic from inelastic deformation (4.5.3). Link: AT 1, AT 2.

PURPOSE: To investigate the effect of varying the force on the acceleration of an object of constant mass, and the effect of varying the mass of an object on the acceleration produced by a constant force (Newton's Second Law, 4.5.6.2.2).
APPARATUS: Trolley, runway (ramp or track) with a pulley at the end, string
Slotted masses (e.g. 10 g) and a mass hanger
Two light gates connected to a data logger (or one light gate with an interrupt card; or ticker timer and tape)
Interrupt card of known length, balance, metre rule
A buffer or block at the end of the track; eye protection
METHOD: Set up the trolley on the runway, with the string over the pulley to the hanger. Compensate for friction by tilting the runway slightly until the trolley moves at constant speed when given a small push.
Measure the mass of the trolley and each slotted mass. Place several slotted masses on the trolley; the total mass of trolley + masses + hanger is kept constant throughout the force investigation.
Force varied: move one slotted mass at a time from the trolley to the hanger so that the accelerating force (weight of the hanging masses) increases while the total mass stays the same.

Release the trolley from the same starting position each time; use the light gates and data logger to measure its speeds and the time between gates (or the speed through each gate) to calculate acceleration, a = (v − u) ÷ t (or v² − u² = 2 a s).
Repeat each force three times and calculate the mean acceleration.
Mass varied: keep the hanging mass (force) constant; add slotted masses to the trolley to increase the total mass; measure the acceleration for each mass.
Plot acceleration (y) against force (x) for part 1 (and against 1 ÷ mass for part 2).
CV: Part 1: total mass of the system; Part 2: hanging mass (force)
Same runway, friction compensation and release position
Same distance between the light gates
SAFETY: Stop the trolley at the end of the runway with a buffer; do not let it fall on feet.
Keep the masses on the hanger low to the floor (use a sand tray/cushion).
Eye protection if the string could snap.
RESULTS: Acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force for a constant mass (a straight line through the origin).
For a constant force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (a against mass is a curve; a against 1/mass is a straight line through the origin).
ANALYSIS: F = m a (4.5.6.2.2); a = F ÷ m; compare a measured from the gradient with the value predicted from the total mass.
Acceleration from the data logger: a = Δv ÷ t; from the gradient of a velocity–time graph.
Resultant force = weight of the hanging masses = m g (g is given).
ERRORS: Friction (runway, pulley, axles) – compensate by tilting the runway and use a low-friction pulley.
The hanging masses also accelerate, so the total mass accelerated must include them – keep the total constant when varying force.
Human reaction time if timing by hand – use light gates and a data logger.
Interrupt card length and release position inconsistent – use the same card and position.
Tilting the runway too far gives a component of weight down the slope – check the trolley moves at constant speed only.
EXAM: Describe how to vary force while keeping mass constant (and vice versa) and why moving masses from the trolley to the hanger does this.
Why compensate for friction? State the conclusion from a graph; calculate acceleration from F = m a.
Explain how light gates and data logger measure speed and acceleration. Link: AT 1, AT 2, AT 3.

PURPOSE: To make observations to identify the suitability of apparatus to measure the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and waves in a solid, and to take appropriate measurements (4.6.1.2).
APPARATUS: Ripple tank with a motor-driven dipper (or straight vibrator), lamp above the tank, white screen/paper below, shallow water, metre rule
Strobe light (or a camera/video, or a slow-motion setting) to freeze the wave pattern
For a solid: signal generator and vibration transducer, a stretched string/elastic cord (or a metre of spring) over a pulley with a hanging mass, metre rule, stopwatch
Eye protection
METHOD: Ripple tank: set up the tank with a shallow layer of water; switch on the dipper at a known frequency so that straight (or circular) waves travel across the tank.

Use the strobe (or take a photograph/video) to make the pattern appear stationary. Place the ruler on the screen; measure the length of, say, 5–10 wavelengths and divide by the number of wavelengths to find the wavelength λ.

Find the frequency f from the motor's setting, or count the number of waves passing a point in a measured time. Calculate the wave speed v = f λ (or measure the distance a wave front travels in a measured time).

Solid: attach the vibration transducer to one end of the string; connect it to the signal generator. Adjust the frequency until a stationary wave with clear nodes is seen. Measure the distance between several nodes: the wavelength = 2 × the distance between neighbouring nodes. Read f from the generator and calculate v = f λ.
Repeat at different frequencies and calculate the mean wave speed; note which apparatus makes the observation easiest and most accurate (suitability of apparatus).
CV: Depth of the water (ripple tank); tension and length of the string (solid)
Position where the wavelength is measured
SAFETY: Keep mains electrical equipment away from water; use low-voltage supply for the lamp/dipper and dry hands.
Strobe lights can trigger photosensitive epilepsy – warn anyone who may be affected.
Mop up spills immediately (slip hazard); avoid hanging masses that could fall on feet.
RESULTS: The wave pattern appears stationary under a strobe at a matching frequency; the wavelength decreases as the frequency increases (v ≈ constant for the same depth).
For the string, nodes are evenly spaced, with higher frequency giving more loops and shorter wavelength.
ANALYSIS: v = f λ (wave equation); f = 1 ÷ T; wavelength from distance ÷ number of waves.
Example: 5 waves span 0.20 m so λ = 0.040 m; f = 12 Hz gives v = 0.48 m/s.
ERRORS: Measuring a single wavelength has a large percentage uncertainty – measure across several wavelengths.
Judging when the pattern is stationary – adjust the strobe carefully; use a camera and freeze-frame.
Waves reflecting from the sides of the tank interfere – use a beach (absorber) at the edges.
Frequency of the generator may not be exact; calibrate with a stopwatch count.
EXAM: Describe how to measure the wavelength, frequency and speed of water ripples (and why the strobe/camera is used).
Describe a method to measure the speed of ripples on a water surface (AT 1, AT 4) and of sound in air (see 4.6.1.2).
Calculate v = f λ; explain why measuring several wavelengths improves accuracy. Link: AT 4.

PURPOSE: (Physics only) To investigate the reflection of light by different types of surface and the refraction of light by different substances (4.6.1.3).
APPARATUS: Ray box with single slit and low-voltage power supply
Plane mirror, different surfaces (e.g. shiny and rough/matt), rectangular glass or Perspex block, semicircular block, a clear water-filled block (optional)
White paper, sharp pencil, ruler, protractor
Eye protection
METHOD: Reflection: draw a straight line on paper and a normal at 90° to it; place the mirror along the line. Shine a thin ray from the ray box at the mirror along a marked angle of incidence i (measured from the normal). Mark the incident ray and the reflected ray with dots and join them; measure the angle of reflection r. Repeat for 5–6 angles; plot r against i.

Different surfaces: shine the ray onto a smooth shiny surface and a rough surface; observe the reflected light (a single direction for a smooth surface – specular; scattered for a rough surface – diffuse).

Refraction: place the rectangular block on paper and draw round it. Shine a ray into one side at an angle i; mark the ray entering and leaving the block. Remove the block and join the dots to show the ray inside the block; draw the normal and measure the angle of refraction r. Repeat for several angles and for blocks made from different substances.
Compare the paths of the rays; plot r against i for each substance.
IV: Angle of incidence (or type of surface/substance).
DV: Angle of reflection or angle of refraction (or observed type of reflection).
CV: Same ray box slit and distance from block
Same procedure for marking the angles; same thickness of block (when comparing substances)
SAFETY: Ray box lamps become hot – do not touch and allow to cool.
Glass blocks have sharp edges and break easily – handle with care.
Darkened rooms – watch for trip hazards; do not look directly into the lamp.
RESULTS: Reflection: angle of reflection = angle of incidence for all surfaces; smooth surfaces give specular reflection, rough surfaces give diffuse reflection.

Refraction: entering a denser medium (air → glass) the ray bends towards the normal; leaving it bends away; a ray along the normal does not bend. The emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways. Different substances bend the light by different amounts.
ANALYSIS: Measure angles from the normal, not from the surface. A graph of r against i is a straight line of gradient 1 for reflection.
Refraction is due to the change in wave speed on entering a different medium (explanatory; HT wave front explanation in 4.6.2.2).
ERRORS: A wide ray makes marking dots uncertain – use a thin slit and mark dots far apart.
Protractor parallax and thick pencil lines – use a sharp pencil and read at eye level.
Placing the block inconsistently – draw round it and do not move it.
Improve by repeating angles and drawing the lines with a ruler.
EXAM: Describe the method and name the normal, angle of incidence and angle of refraction (and mark them on a diagram).
State the law of reflection; describe what happens when light enters/leaves a glass block; distinguish specular and diffuse reflection (4.6.2.6).
Why use a thin ray? Why measure angles from the normal? Link: AT 4, AT 8.

PURPOSE: To investigate how the amount of infrared radiation absorbed or radiated by a surface depends on the nature of that surface (4.6.2.2).
APPARATUS: Leslie cube (hollow metal cube with four different faces – shiny silver, matt black, shiny black, matt white) and hot water (kettle); or two identical metal cans (one painted matt black, one shiny silver) with lids
Infrared detector (thermopile with meter, or an infrared thermometer/heat sensor), ruler
Thermometers or temperature probes, stopwatch, measuring cylinder
Heat lamp, two identical metal plates or tubes with different surfaces (for the absorption investigation)
Eye protection
METHOD: Radiated (emission): fill the Leslie cube with boiling/very hot water (the same temperature for all faces). Place the infrared detector at a fixed distance (e.g. 10 cm) from the first face, record the reading, then turn the cube and repeat for each face at the same distance. Repeat readings.

Alternative for radiated: fill the two identical cans with the same volume of hot water at the same starting temperature; record the temperature of each every minute for about 10 minutes; compare the cooling.
Absorbed: place identical plates (one matt black, one shiny silver) equal distances from a heat source (a lamp) with a thermometer fixed behind each; record the temperature rise over a fixed time.
Compare the readings for the different surfaces.
IV: The nature of the surface (colour/texture: matt black, shiny black, white, silver).
DV: Amount of infrared radiation detected (meter reading) or the temperature change of the object.
CV: Temperature of the hot surfaces/water at the start
Distance and angle of the detector (or heat source) from the surface
Area of the surfaces; time of exposure; same container size/material
SAFETY: Boiling water and the cube are hot – carry carefully; use a kettle safely; allow to cool before handling.
Heat lamps get very hot – keep fingers and cables away.
Wear eye protection; mop up spills at once.
RESULTS: The matt black surface emits (and absorbs) the most infrared radiation; the shiny silver surface emits (and absorbs) the least. Matt white lies between them. Good absorbers are good emitters; shiny surfaces are poor absorbers and poor emitters (reflecting more).
ANALYSIS: Rank the surfaces by detector reading (or temperature change); calculate means of repeats; present in a bar chart (MS 2c).
Draw a conclusion linking surface, absorption and emission to black body ideas (4.6.3.1, physics only).
ERRORS: The detector distance or angle varies – clamp it at a fixed distance.
The cube cools during the investigation – work quickly, take the readings in a set order, or take readings in several rotations.
Other sources of infrared (hands, lamps, sunlight) – shield the detector, keep it away from other hot objects.
The thermometer's resolution – use a temperature probe; repeat three times.
EXAM: Which surface radiates most infrared at the same temperature? Explain the results using absorption/emission of infrared.
Why keep the detector at a fixed distance? Why use the same temperature for each surface?
Draw a bar chart and conclusion. Link: AT 1, AT 4; also 4.6.3.1 (physics only).
